summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 1100 through RFC 1199, written as a status report. It marks which ones are on the standards track and points to the IAB list for current status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a table of contents for one hundred notebooks, with a line about each one.

subtitle: An annotated guide to 100 RFCs documenting the standards and developments of the early Internet.

tldr.problem: Readers need to understand what each of the 100 RFCs from 1100 to 1199 is about and its standards status.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents a brief summary and status note for each RFC in that range, marking which ones advance the standards track and pointing to the official standards document for current status.
tldr.outcome: The summary provides a snapshot of Internet protocol and documentation work in 1991, serving as a historical record and quick reference for the RFCs of that era.

today: RFC 1199 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It serves as a historical record of Internet standards work in 1991, preserved for reference. Readers seeking current RFC status should consult the latest RFC 3000 (Internet Official Protocol Standards) document.

sections.title: What This RFC Is
sections.content:
RFC 1199 is a brief annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered from 1100 through 1199. The author, Joyce Reynolds, writes one sentence or a short paragraph about each RFC to explain its subject, its purpose, and whether it is on the Internet standards track.

The RFC notes that standards status can change over time, so it points readers to the official IAB Official Protocol Standards document for the current state of any RFC on the standards track.
sections.eli5: It is basically a teacher handing you a list that says: 'Here are 100 notebooks. Here is one sentence about what is in each one.'

sections.title: The 100 RFCs and Their Subjects
sections.content:
The RFCs from 1100 to 1199 cover a wide range of Internet topics. Many are on the standards track, covering protocols like TCP/IP extensions (such as TCP header compression), network management (SNMP), routing protocols (OSPF, BGP, IS-IS), electronic mail improvements (Privacy Enhanced Mail, X.400 mapping), and emerging protocols like Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) for serial links.

Others are informational, providing guidance to network managers, explaining the Internet governance structure (the Internet Activities Board), documenting network security incidents (such as the 1988 Internet worm), and publishing workshop reports and policy discussions.
sections.eli5: The RFCs in this batch cover many different topics: how computers send messages to each other, how networks keep track of the best paths, how to keep email private, and how people decide what the rules of the Internet should be.

sections.title: Standards-Track RFCs
sections.content:
RFCs on the standards track are marked with [STANDARDS-TRACK] in the summary. These include foundational protocols and updates to existing standards. Examples from this batch include RFC 1122 (Host Requirements for Internet Hosts), RFC 1171 (Point-to-Point Protocol), RFC 1158 (Management Information Base, MIB-II), and RFC 1131 (OSPF, the Open Shortest Path First routing protocol).

The RFC notes that standards status is not static. Some RFCs obsolete earlier ones (such as RFC 1184 obsoleting RFC 1116 for the Telnet Linemode option), and some update others (like RFC 1105, which is updated by RFCs 1163 and 1164 for the Border Gateway Protocol).
sections.eli5: These RFCs mark the rules that Internet computers have to follow. They change over time as people learn what works better.

sections.title: Informational and Historical Documents
sections.content:
Many RFCs in this range are informational, such as RFC 1180 (A TCP/IP Tutorial), RFC 1121 (Act One: The Poems, celebrating the 20th anniversary of the ARPANET), and RFC 1149 (A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers, an April 1st joke). RFC 1178 offers guidelines for choosing names for computers; RFC 1177 documents frequently asked questions about the Internet.

RFC 1135 examines the 1988 Internet worm incident, providing a historical account of what was then called the helminthiasis (parasitic infestation) of the Internet. These documents, though not standards, preserve important context and practical guidance for the Internet community.
sections.eli5: These RFCs are like notebooks that explain things or tell stories about the Internet, but they are not official rules that everyone has to follow.

sections.title: Status and the Standards Process
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the status of RFCs may change during standards processing. An RFC might start as a proposed standard, advance to draft standard, and eventually become a full standard (or be made historic or withdrawn). Because this snapshot was taken in December 1991, readers should consult the latest version of the IAB Official Protocol Standards document to learn the current status of any RFC mentioned.

The document includes RFCs covering diverse maturity levels: some define mature, widely deployed standards, while others are experimental explorations of new ideas. RFC 1186, for example, documents the MD4 Message Digest Algorithm as informational, not yet a standard.
sections.eli5: When a rule is brand new, it is called a proposal. As more people test it and like it, it might become an official rule. This document shows what things were being tried in 1991.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.content:
RFC 1199 is a snapshot of Internet standards work in December 1991, a moment when the Internet was transitioning from a research project to a global infrastructure. The RFCs in this batch reflect debates about routing (BGP and OSPF replacing simpler protocols), the move from simple interior gateway protocols (RIP) to more scalable ones, and the growth of network management complexity.

Later readers can use this summary to understand the state of Internet standards at a specific point in time. The mixture of standards-track and experimental RFCs shows how the Internet evolved: some ideas (like PPP and BGP) became foundational, while others (like TCP Big Window extensions or certain mail mapping schemes) did not gain wide adoption.
sections.eli5: This document is like a time capsule. It shows what the Internet community was working on and thinking was important in 1991.
